_comment: Which captured image backs which finding, and what the reviewer is looking at. A finding with no image says so rather than borrowing one.

F-01.caption: The script requested /pm and landed on /pm/event/atp-faria-alcaraz-2026-09-02. The stored tab in localStorage reopened the previous market and rewrote the address bar.

F-02.caption: A real Chromium window on the live application, showing one market record whose own fields disagree about whether play has happened, from the live response fetched by this browser.

F-03.caption: Settlement Time reads Sep 9, 3:00 PM UTC on a market that shows a final score of 2-6, is marked Resolved, and has its order book closed. The match was played on 2 September.

F-04.caption: A real Chromium window on the live application, with outcomes that accept orders while carrying no price of any kind counted from the live API response fetched by this same browser.

F-05.caption: The default Trending grid, which is where resolved markets are promoted with live buy buttons.

F-06.caption: A real Chromium window on the live application, comparing stored probabilities against the percentage the interface can display, from the live response fetched by this browser.

F-07.caption: Every prop label repeats the full event title before the part that identifies it, so the rail truncates exactly where the distinguishing text begins. 48 rows carry the prefix.

F-08.caption: The same rail, showing 13 rows rendering "-- Vol" beside neighbours that show $4K Vol and $116 Vol.

F-09.caption: A real Chromium window on the live /pm page, with the console messages the browser itself raised during this load counted and quoted from that same load.

F-11.caption: Both 2028 cards render in this grid at the same time, one spelling the candidate "J.D. Vance" and the other "JD Vance".

F-12.caption: Before: a search for bitcoin has narrowed the grid to matching markets, and the query is in the box.
After one click on the Politics chip: the search box is empty and the query is gone. Read back from the DOM immediately afterwards, both search inputs returned an empty string.

F-13.caption: The subcategory rail, where entries showing a count of 0 are still offered as selectable filters.

F-14.caption: At 375x812 the subcategory rail scrolls horizontally, so the filter responsible for an empty result can sit off-screen with no control to clear it.

F-15.caption: The directory whose inactive responsive layout stays focusable at zero size, putting invisible stops in the keyboard tab order ahead of the first market card.

F-16.caption: The nav reads "August Rewards", captured with the browser clock in the same run at 2026-09-03T09:46:37Z.

F-18.caption: app.manic.trade/pm rendering inside an iframe on a page served from an unrelated origin. The market grid, live prices and the Log In button are all present, and the browser raised no framing objection.

F-19.caption: A real Chromium window on the live /pm page. The band lists the security headers actually returned on this very page load, read from the response as it arrived; the application is rendering underneath, unmodified.

F-20.caption: A real Chromium window after requesting an invented market slug. The HTTP status and document size are the ones this request actually received; the application renders as if the market were real.

F-21.caption: A real Chromium window on the live application, showing outcome names that differ only by capitalisation inside one live response.

F-22.caption: A real Chromium window on the live /pm page. The heading, landmark and image-alt counts are read from the DOM of the page visible underneath at the moment of capture.

F-23.caption: A real Chromium window on the live application, showing the share metadata a link to /pm actually carries, read from the HTML this browser was served.

F-24.caption: A real Chromium window after requesting a route that correctly returns 404, showing the status and the size of the body sent to say so.

F-25.caption: A real Chromium window on /pm, with the byte offsets of the title and Open Graph tags measured inside the HTML this browser was served.

F-26.caption: A real Chromium window on the live application, showing a market reported as finished that is still counting down to a close days in the future.

F-27.caption: A real Chromium window on the live /pm page. The transfer figures come from the page’s own Resource Timing entries for this load, set against the number of cards actually in the DOM.

F-28.caption: A real Chromium window on the live /referral page, with the h1 elements found in that page’s own DOM listed and quoted.

F-29.caption: A real Chromium window on the live application, showing the distribution of gaps between a match starting and its market closing, with the spike at exactly seven days.

F-30.caption: A real Chromium window on the live /pm page, showing the promotion label present in the navigation at capture time alongside the capture date.

F-31.caption: A real Chromium window on the live landing page. The count of interactive controls carrying no accessible name is read from the DOM of the page shown underneath.

F-32.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response for a match the API marks finished, with acceptingOrders still true on that same record.

F-33.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response, with the markets past their end time yet still accepting orders counted and listed from that same response.

F-34.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response for an event whose end timestamp precedes its own start timestamp, with both dates resolved.

F-35.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response for an outcome marked inactive while still accepting orders.

F-36.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response where a 24-hour volume exceeds the all-time volume on the same record.

F-37.caption: A real Chromium window after requesting /.well-known/security.txt, showing the status actually returned for the path RFC 9116 reserves for a disclosure contact.

F-38.caption: A real Chromium window after requesting /manifest.json. The status and content-type are the ones returned to this request; the body is the application HTML shell.

F-39.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response, comparing the percentage displayed to a user against the mid of the order book in that same payload.

F-40.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response, with the image hosts counted across that payload.

F-41.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response for an event carrying two outcomes under one identical name.

F-42.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response for finished matches, with the outcomes still carrying a buy price listed from that same payload. No order was placed.

F-43.caption: A real Chromium window showing the live events API response, with total, count and hasMore contradicting each other inside that single response.
